subject: physics
title: Hadrons: Baryons and Mesons
welcome_lead: Pack quarks into threes for baryons or pairs for mesons.
meta_desc: A-Level Particle Physics adventure on hadrons, baryons, mesons and conservation rules.
final_note: Quark composition must give the observed charge — and baryon number must be conserved.

concepts.def: Particle made of quarks; feels strong force.

walkthroughs.body_html: Baryons consist of three quarks. Proton = uud (charge +1). Neutron = udd (charge 0). Both have baryon number B = +1.
Mesons consist of one quark and one antiquark. Pions and kaons are the most common. All mesons have B = 0 and are short-lived.
In every reaction: charge, baryon number, lepton number conserve. Strangeness conserved in strong/EM but can change by ±1 in weak interactions.

mcqs.q: Baryon number of a proton is:
Which of the following is a fundamental particle: proton, electron, or neutron?
options: Only the electron — protons and neutrons are made of quarks.
Only the proton is fundamental; electrons and neutrons are composite.
All three (proton, electron, neutron) are fundamental particles that cannot be broken down.
Electrons are sometimes waves and sometimes particles depending on the temperature of the apparatus.

mcqs.q: When does an electron behave as a wave?
options: In experiments that probe wave properties (e.g. diffraction through a crystal); in particle-like experiments it behaves as a particle.
Electrons are sometimes waves and sometimes particles depending on the temperature of the apparatus.
Electrons are always waves and only look like particles at low energy.

mcqs.q: If an object is moving at constant velocity in a straight line, what is the net force on it?
options: There must be a forward force on the object to keep it moving.
Zero — by Newton's first law, constant velocity requires zero net force.
Only the proton is fundamental; electrons and neutrons are composite.
The net force equals the velocity times the mass of the object.
